name: Neck hammock / cervical stretcher

card.summary: Over-door neck traction harness borrowed from physical therapy; sold for posture, but research covers neck pain, not looks.
card.note: Clinical cervical traction is supervised; evidence for neck pain is low quality.

quick.overview:
A neck hammock is a home version of cervical traction: a harness around the head and chin connected to a pulley or inflatable collar that pulls the head upward and away from the shoulders.

It is marketed for neck tension and forward-head posture. Published research on traction concerns neck pain and radiculopathy rather than appearance.
quick.mechanism: The device applies a pulling force along the cervical spine, aiming to separate vertebrae and stretch surrounding soft tissue, as clinical mechanical traction does.[1]
quick.risks: Guidelines for cervical traction rest on low-quality evidence and dosing is unresolved. The sources consulted do not catalogue adverse effects.[1]

lead: A neck hammock, also sold as an over-the-door cervical traction device, is a home product with a head harness, straps and a pulley or door mount that applies a gentle upward pull along the neck. People use it to stretch the neck and upper back, and posture-focused communities promote it for countering forward head posture, in which the ear sits ahead of the shoulder line and the chin juts forward.[1][2]

It is a consumer version of cervical traction, a physical-therapy technique used to separate the neck vertebrae and stretch soft tissue.[1] Wikipedia describes forward head posture as most often linked to prolonged use of laptops and phones, with the head's forward position increasing the load on the neck.[2] An upright head-over-shoulders alignment is what people hope to see in photos and profile views.

Published literature on cervical traction mostly concerns neck pain and cervical radiculopathy. Reviews report that traction combined with other physical therapy is described as reducing pain, while guidelines for cervical radiculopathy rest on low-quality evidence and optimal dosage remains unresolved.[1] A few small trials of posture-correcting extension traction have studied forward head posture in specific patient groups.[3]

chain: Harness applies an upward pull to the cervical spine
Users aim for a head positioned over the shoulders and a longer-looking neck
angle.text: The device is used with the aim of easing the forward-head position so the head sits more over the shoulders, which changes how the neck and jaw line look from the side. Published studies of traction measure pain and alignment in clinical groups, not appearance.

infobox: Head harness with straps and a door-mounted pulley or inflatable collar

paras: Over-door versions attach a pulley to the top of a door and hang a weight or bag from a rope that runs to a chin-and-occiput harness. Clinical mechanical traction uses an apparatus that applies force intermittently or continuously, with stated goals including separating vertebral bodies, moving facet joints, widening the intervertebral foramen and stretching soft tissues.[1]

Forward head posture is described as an excessively flexed upper spine with the head poked forward, the ear ahead of the shoulder line and the chin forward. Wikipedia links it to prolonged use of small devices and to certain occupations, and lists strengthening of mid and lower back and deep neck flexors, stretching of the upper trapezius, mobilization and ergonomic changes among treatment approaches; it does not discuss traction by name.[2]
Research listed on the page includes a 2019 systematic review linking forward head posture with neck pain in adults but not adolescents.[2]

No studies found of neck hammocks specifically for posture or appearance. Studies of clinical cervical traction exist for neck pain and radiculopathy. A 2020 review by Colombo and colleagues, as summarised on Wikipedia, found mechanical traction outperformed manual traction, and described the pain-relief effect as statistically significant but not clinically relevant.[1]

Published randomized trials have examined forward head posture correction in specific groups, including a 2025 pilot trial using a cervical extension traction orthotic in temporomandibular disorders, a 2023 trial comparing two corrective approaches in older adults with neck pain, and 2021 and 2022 trials of cervical alignment restoration for headache and radiculopathy.[3]

The sources consulted do not list adverse effects of cervical traction. General traction guidance mentions neurovascular checks, and clinical traction is delivered under professional supervision with defined force, rhythm, duration and frequency.[1]
